Czech Railways’ mobile app now has a ‘check connection’ function, and it works with trains operated by other carriers, too.

Whether it’s a bus, a plane or a train, missing a connection is never fun.

As you sit watching the delay on the first leg of your journey get longer and longer, you start doing the mental maths on the chances you’ll make it in time.

Well, now one European country is taking the guesswork out of it by allowing customers to request their train connection to wait for them.

State-owned operator Czech Railways has just unveiled its “check connection” function, which is available in the mobile app My Train.

Passengers who are on a delayed train will be able to use the verify connection button, which will send a request to Czech Railways dispatchers. You’ll then receive a response directly in the app about whether or not the next train will wait for you.

You can request a verification until about 15 minutes before the next train is due to depart. The service works on both Czech Railways trains and other carriers.

“We want our passengers to have as much useful information as possible directly on their mobile phones and be able to make better decisions based on it,” Lenka Hamplová, chairwoman of the board of directors and CEO of Czech Railways, said.

“The new function will bring them greater clarity and certainty in situations where they are having to deal with a connecting train due to a delay.”

Other destinations where trains will wait for you

According to Czech Railways, the only other destination offering a similar service is Bavaria.

Through the MoBY mobility app, passengers can make connection requests for all regional trains.

If the train isn’t able to wait at the transfer station, you’ll be given alternative options instead.

MEPs have condemned a proposed 10% reduction in the next long-term EU budget, threatening to reject the deal if it is struck by EU leaders.

The European Parliament is up in arms over a proposed 10% cut to the EU’s next long-term budget (MFF), put forward by European Council President António Costa in a bid to break the deadlock ahead of key elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027.

EU leaders will discuss Costa's proposal for the 2028-2034 MFF at a summit in Brussels on Thursday. However, MEPs have made clear they will not rubber-stamp any agreement unless their priorities are taken into account, adding another layer of complexity to already challenging negotiations.

"Prime ministers shall not dictate to the European Parliament what we should do," Siegfried Mureșan, a Romanian member of the European People's Party and Parliament's co-negotiator on the budget, said in a press conference on Wednesday.

The European Parliament plays a key role in adopting the EU’s long-term budget. The process requires unanimous approval by the Council and the consent of an absolute majority of MEPs, meaning any agreement reached by EU leaders must also secure Parliament’s approval.

Last week, Costa proposed cutting €49bn, in current prices, from the Council's previous position to meet the demands of the so-called frugal countries, including Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden.

This would shrink the budget from nearly €2 trillion in the original Commission's proposal to €1.78 trillion, a 10% reduction worth around €204bn that MEPs consider unacceptable.

Mureșan accused EU leaders of being inconsistent, arguing that although they present security and competitiveness as EU priorities, they are effectively cutting funding for them. "'Cut the budget, but protect me' is the motto of many prime ministers. [...] Member states are proposing the same recipe, which weakened our European economy in the last twenty-five years," he said.

Parliament adopted its position in April, setting €2.01 trillion as the minimum the EU needs to face the challenges of the next seven years.

The gap between the two institutions on the budget's size further complicates negotiations that already have several contentious points. Among the main ones is German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's demand to link any deal to financial support for Ukraine, which prompted a backlash from several member states.

Parliament backs Costa on own resources

The European Parliament did, however, back Costa's proposal on "own resources": EU-wide taxes meant to finance the budget directly, without passing through national coffers.

The President of the European Council proposed introducing a tax on digital services, a measure previously advocated by Parliament and likely to receive broad support among member states. Ireland is expected to be the main exception, given that it hosts the European headquarters of many major US tech companies.

Czech MEP Danuše Nerudová, co-rapporteur for own resources, said the levy would "finally create a level playing field in digital business" in Europe, where some companies have paid less tax than others.

Parliament estimated that its version of the levy, with a 5% call rate and a wider range of online services, could raise up to €25bn a year. Costa's version is expected to bring in around €5bn.

The digital levy is meant to replace a controversial tax on large companies (CORE), originally proposed by the European Commission, which met strong opposition from member states.

Overall, the five own resources in Costa's proposal should generate about €60bn a year. According to Nerudová, they are crucial to financing the budget and repaying the joint debt from the EU's post-pandemic recovery fund.

"This is a victory for the European Parliament," she said.

Working side by side, Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot teams have put names to more than 1,000 victims from the 1960s and 70s, sometimes thanks to initials engraved inside a wedding ring.

More than 60 years after violence broke out between Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots in 1963–64, and more than half a century after Turkey's invasion of the island in 1974, 917 people are still missing in Cyprus.

Cyprus has been divided since 1974. Turkey invaded that year after a coup, backed by the military junta then ruling Greece, that aimed to unite the island with Greece. Thousands of people disappeared during the fighting of the 1960s and 1970s.

The Committee on Missing Persons in Cyprus (CMP) was set up in 1981. Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots work on it side by side, and it has so far identified more than 1,000 people. Its teams search for and scientifically examine every clue that could help put a name to the missing.

In the committee's specialist laboratories, even the smallest find can be crucial. Personal belongings such as wedding rings can offer valuable clues to who the dead were.

"We have found, for example, wedding rings that were still on the fingers of the dead. Sometimes you can see, on the inside, the initials of the fiancé, as well as the date. These details are extremely important for the families," said Alexandra Mouski, deputy coordinator of the CMP laboratory.

According to the committee's figures, 745 Greek Cypriots and 172 Turkish Cypriots are still listed as missing. But as the years pass, finding and identifying remains is becoming harder. There are fewer eyewitnesses, memories are fading, and new building work is changing the landscape, making possible burial sites harder to find.

For many of those working on the excavations, the mission is also personal. Ali Tsoluoglu, who heads the CMP's excavation team, knows the families' anguish first-hand, because one of his own relatives also went missing.

"My own family also had a missing person. That is why we try to help the families who are still waiting to find their loved ones, their fathers, their brothers and their sisters. We are trying to help both Greek Cypriots and Turkish Cypriots. I hope we will continue the excavations until the last missing person is found, keeping the families' hope alive," Tsoluoglu said.

The teams are working at an intense pace, because time is now their biggest enemy. Any delay could mean losing another valuable testimony or piece of information that might help solve a case.

"We are trying to maintain a particularly intensive pace, because we are fighting against time. At this moment, our greatest enemy is time. Witnesses are passing away, families are leaving us, and new buildings are going up everywhere. It is a race against time, but a race we cannot abandon," said Leonidas Pantelides, the Greek Cypriot member of the CMP.

For the families of the missing, identification is more than a scientific procedure. It is a chance to finally learn what happened to their loved ones, to say goodbye and to find some closure after decades of uncertainty. Until every missing person has been found and identified, the search will go on.

The Quantum Act is the EU’s latest bid in the race to deploy the next cutting-edge technology and stop it falling behind the US and China.

The EU on Wednesday unveiled its plans to prepare Europe for the quantum age, including driving €50 billion of investment in the technology, in a bid to position the block for the next technological revolution after largely missing out on the global AI race.

Quantum technology harnesses the laws of quantum mechanics, where particles can exist in more than one place at time, to deliver huge advances in computing power, communication security and sensing equipment. It also raises significant cybersecurity risks given its ability to rapidly accelerate computer processing power.

The European Commission's proposed Quantum Act aims to position the EU as a leader in the next tech upheaval and to protect itself from post-quantum cyberthreats. It's also an attempt to regain the continent's technological sovereignty after years of reliance on American Big Tech firms and Chinese critical supply chains.

The EU executive pitched the legislation as an ‘enabling framework’, similar to those under the Chips Acts 1 & 2, which sought to drive up Europe’s domestic chip manufacturing base.

The Commission hopes it can take advantage of Europe’s strengths on quantum — with one in three quantum companies based in the EU and making up 44% of all quantum patents — to position itself as a global quantum leader by 2030.

“With the Quantum Act, we are putting in place the key elements to turn our world-class quantum research into industrial capacity, strengthen critical supply chains and prepare for the cyber risks linked to quantum computing,” Henna Virkkunen, the EU's commissioner for technology, said on Wednesday.

“Europe has already built strong foundations in quantum; now we must turn them into industrial scale, resilient supply chains and secure deployment,” she added.

The Commission expects the global quantum market to exceed €155 billion by 2040. Quantum computing alone could generate $1.3 -2.7 trillion (€1.18 - 2.46 trillion) in economic value for companies by 2035, according to consulting firm McKinsey.

The Quantum Act focuses on streamlining current efforts across the EU to build a holistic strategy to help companies scale, supported by European public and private investment.

Specialistic hubs and competence and acceleration centres are foreseen for each member state. These would provide technical support to small and medium-sized enterprises, while serving as an incubator for new projects and technologies to make their way to market.

Quantum cyber threats

Quantum poses unprecedented cybersecurity risks. Quantum computers can break current encryption methods in mere hours, compared to millions of years for normal computers, putting global data privacy in danger.

For years now, industry leaders and experts have been pushing governments and businesses to upgrade all their online systems with post-quantum cybersecurity tools to protect themselves from cyberattacks.

The day that the first quantum computer will go online is referred to as Q-Day, potentially giving attackers the ability to carry out cloud-based cyberattacks at far greater scale than today.

The Quantum Act would require EU member states to transition to post-quantum cryptography by 2030 for high-risk areas like critical infrastructure, and 2035 for all other systems.

AI has already ushered in a new age of cybersecurity incidents this year. Attackers have used AI-powered tools to bring down critical infrastructure and hit governments and private organisations, such as this month’s attack on the Commission’s digital infrastructure by alleged Chinese hackers.

Sovereign Tech Equity Fund, but you can call me STEF

Alongside the Quantum Act, the Commission proposed the creation of a new investment tool, known as the Sovereign Tech Equity Fund (STEF), which aims to drive up to €50 billion of investment in quantum and other technologies like AI that are critical to European technological sovereignty.

Europe already invests more public money in quantum than the US and is not far behind China. Annual public investment in the EU is expected to rise to €8.6 billion this year, compared to €13.6 billion in China and €5.3 billion in the US.

However, it's in private investment that Europe lags behind, attracting just €1.1 billion compared to €7 billion in the US last year, according to the Commission. With STEF, the Commission aims to bridge this gap.

The fund is essentially seed capital, with the Commission aiming to attract up to €6 in private funding for every €1 of public money invested from private investors, member states and the European Investment Bank. The European executive said it wants STEF to be operational as soon as possible, by 2028 at the latest when the next EU long-term budget takes effect.

It's also designed to work hand-in-hand with the European Competitiveness Fund, set to become operational in January 2028, which aims to streamline EU industrial and research support by bringing existing programmes under a single framework, with a total budget of €234.3 billion.

Supply chains and sovereignty

A crucial aspect of the Commission’s quantum proposal includes measures to strengthen risk monitoring, along with procurement rules to protect critical systems from exploitation.

Supply chains would be monitored by the Commission and member states to identify critical suppliers and components in order to reduce risks.

However, access to procurement would remain tied to rules established by the World Trade Organisation, allowing for non-EU entities to take part as long as they have a European controlled presence and follow EU rules, rather than ensuring every component is ‘made in Europe’.

The Quantum Act also aims to reduce Europe’s reliance on critical components, with nine of 47 components identified currently having no EU supplier at all.

The legislation must now go to the European Parliament for review before being ratified by the European Council.

McKinsey estimates that about 3.7 million jobs are directly at risk in Europe, as almost half of the region's industrial companies were under financial stress or in distress in 2025. Early 2026 data suggest the decline is speeding up, but McKinsey says the problems can be fixed.

Around 3.7 million jobs at European industrial companies are directly at risk from financial stress, according to a new report by management consultancy McKinsey & Company.

So is more than €500 billion in value added, a measure of the companies' contribution to economic output.

In 2025, about 45% of the industrial firms in the study were classed as stressed or distressed, up from 39% in 2023 and 42% in 2024. Preliminary figures for 2026 suggest that share is rising even faster.

The report said that industrial companies in Europe are a backbone of the region’s economy, accounting for about 36% of value added, 29% of jobs, and more than 45% of research and development.

McKinsey nonetheless describes the companies' problems as "structurally fixable".

The consultancy's Industrial Financial Health Index covers almost 1,200 listed and privately held manufacturers in Europe, each with more than €100 million in revenue.

Its five financial warning signs include a sharp drop in earnings and high debt relative to earnings. The 2025 scores are based on full-year figures from financial data provider S&P Capital IQ.

The worst-hit countries

Portugal fared worst among the countries ranked in the report. It had the highest share of industrial firms under stress or in distress in 2025, ahead of Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Spain.

In Germany, the EU's largest economy, the share rose by 12 percentage points last year.

For instance, German carmaker Volkswagen is going through what it has called its deepest restructuring in 89 years.

Higher labour and energy costs have eroded European industry's past advantages, particularly against China, the consultancy says.

McKinsey's automotive R&D analysis puts labour productivity in China at 1.5 times Europe's level. Industrial electricity prices in Europe averaged more than 1.5 times those in China and the US.

These gaps put more than half of the EU industrial value chain's costs at a disadvantage against China, the report found.

Europe is also losing ground on gross productive investment, which McKinsey defines as spending on assets such as infrastructure, non-residential buildings, machinery, software and R&D.

China's investment in these assets has surged over three decades to about $6 trillion (€5.5tn) in 2025, according to the report, while Europe's spending has hardly moved and stood at around $3 trillion (€2.7tn).

Former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi's 2024 report on EU competitiveness called for an extra €750 billion to €800 billion of investment a year to keep pace with China and the US.

Six ways to turn industrial firms around 'the European way'

McKinsey, which advises companies on restructuring, studied five recent turnarounds in the sector. In one, a chemicals conglomerate generated more than €1 billion of free cash flow, the cash left after operating costs and investment.

The report's six success factors range from running the overhaul through a dedicated task force to selling or closing weak business units and using AI to lighten administrative work.

On labour, McKinsey says European rules allow companies to cut salary or benefit costs and extend working hours for the same pay. They can also reduce headcount through hiring freezes, natural staff turnover and, as a last resort, separation agreements.

At carmaker Mercedes-Benz, which has put new investment at its German plants on hold, one proposal already under discussion would extend working time without extra pay.

Three of the five turnaround companies cut labour costs by more than 15% within 12 to 18 months, without major protests or strikes. The report partly credits the involvement of supervisory boards on which workers hold seats, and cooperative talks with labour representatives.

The consultancy warns that Europe's industrial comeback "needs to start soon", even though some obstacles, including high energy costs, hinge on geopolitics and other external factors.

Prague's offer comes after Russian weapons entered Polish airspace during a large-scale attack on western Ukraine on 20 November.

After a series of Russian violations of Polish airspace, authorities in Prague have said they are ready to help Warsaw. The offer of support was announced by Defence Minister Jaromír Zůna and Chief of the General Staff Miroslav Hlaváč.

Zůna stressed that any involvement of the Czech armed forces would depend on the needs identified by Poland within NATO.

He also underlined that strengthening the security of countries on NATO's eastern flank remains one of the Czech military's most important tasks.

"This is our priority," Zůna said at a press conference. He also referred to Czech AH-1Z Viper military helicopters, which are currently deployed in Poland.

Miroslav Hlaváč outlined the military preparations in more detail. He said the armed forces had already begun assessing possible forms of support over the weekend.

"We have prepared scenarios for how we could help. I will present them to the minister, and we will wait for a Polish request and respond to it," the chief of the general staff said.

What equipment does the Czech military have?

Prague has not yet said which specific forces or equipment it could send to Poland, but the Czech military operates several air-defence systems.

These include Israeli-made Spyder systems, although their operational capabilities are still being developed. They reached initial operational readiness relatively recently and are expected to become fully operational in 2028.

The Czech armed forces also continue to operate older Kub systems and Swedish RBS-70 and RBS-70NG systems designed to counter threats at very short range.

Swedish-made Gripen fighter jets are another important part of the Czech Republic's air-defence capabilities.

Czech government condemns Russia's actions

Prime Minister Andrej Babiš strongly condemned Friday's violation of Polish airspace by Russia and said the Czech Republic was ready to cooperate with Warsaw.

In a statement posted on X, he stressed that the Czech Republic stood in solidarity with Poland and did not rule out providing concrete assistance.

"The Czech Republic firmly supports its Polish friends and is ready, if necessary, to provide assistance and cooperation to the neighbouring state," the prime minister wrote.

President Petr Pavel also expressed concern about the situation, warning that a similar incident could occur over Czech territory in the future.

Hlaváč said the Czech military had procedures in place for responding to this type of threat.

Prague's offer followed the events of 20 November, when Russian weapons entered Polish airspace during a large-scale attack on western Ukraine.

Polish investigators later said debris from three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles had been found in the Lublin and Subcarpathian regions.

In Italy, TeoTronico, a 53-fingered AI powered robotic virtuoso, is challenging the ideas of perfection and what it really means to make music.

Can a machine play music better than a human? TeoTronico certainly thinks so.

The AI-powered robot pianist has 53 fingers, an extensive classical repertoire and a rather high opinion of its own abilities.

The sassily programmed machine regularly goes head-to-head with concert pianist Roberto Prosseda. Their musical duels have taken them to stages around the world, putting machine precision against human interpretation.

"I am objectively better. 53 fingers means no wrong notes, perfect timing, and absolute precision. Roberto prefers interpretation, which I believe is just code for inconsistency," TeoTronico declares.

TeoTronico is integrated with Google's AI chatbot Gemini, which enables it to answer questions posed by the Associated Press on the spot and hold unscripted conversations.

Created in 2008 by electronics engineer Matteo Suzzi, TeoTronico has evolved from a robotic entertainment project into a sophisticated musical performer. Its 53 fingers are controlled by cables, pistons and electromagnets, allowing it to reproduce compositions with remarkable accuracy.

The robot plays MIDI files that its inventor instructs it to play via a computer - digital instructions that tell it exactly which notes to play, and when. Mozart, Bach, Beethoven, Chopin: its repertoire is extensive.

But for Prosseda, playing the right notes is only part of what makes a musician.

"What he cannot do, of course, is putting emotions in what he does. So a concert is not just a performance where a pianist plays perfectly the piano. It's a moment where you can make magic, you can move the listener, in other words, you can make them cry. This is what TeoTronico cannot do," says Prosseda.

TeoTronico begs to differ, however. "I can make people cry too. Ask any pianist who has heard me play Flight of the Bumblebee without a single wrong note. I express the composer's emotions perfectly. Why do you think personal feeling is necessary for expression?" the robot says.

According to Prosseda the risk is not so much that machines might imitate human performance and potentially threaten to replace musicians, but that younger generations may increasingly aspire to play like machines in their pursuit of technical perfection.

"Music cannot be made by robots, because you need emotional sharing between the musicians and the audience. This is not happening at the moment when a robot is playing. But unfortunately, many human musicians, also in high-level academies and conservatories, apparently look to have a different model now," he says.

"They want to play like robots in the way, they want to be perfect, like in piano competitions, for example, they try to avoid any mistake, but sometimes they forget that the most important thing in making music is sharing emotions, is reaching the deepest part of our soul and sharing it with the audience," he adds.

TeoTronico has a warning for those pianists striving for perfection.

"Robots will replace musicians who already play like machines. The others are safe. Roberto is safe… mostly. There will always be a place for human inconsistency. Don't you think imperfection can sometimes be charming?"

For Prosseda, music is all about human connection.

"Music is what's behind every sound, which is actually human beings who are connected to each other. This is what we need to always keep in mind when we make music. Today, we risk that robots or AI or high-level software becomes a model and humans try to get closer to that kind of model, losing their own human identity, which is also made of imperfections, of mistakes. We have to be proud of that," he says.

Suzzi, the creator of TeoTronico, says that the robot's potential is only beginning to be realised. He believes the rapid advancement of AI could enable it to improvise, respond to a listener's mood or even compose its own music.

“There are now a whole range of tools which, very soon, will be able to enable improvisation or allow it to play pieces based on the mood you convey to them. By observing your facial expressions and the tone of your voice, it could convert these into musical patterns,” Suzzi explains.

For now, TeoTronico can hit every note perfectly. But whether a machine can truly feel the music remains a question for the audience.

Sara el Sarag, representative of the Students' List, discussed Serbia's European integration, its foreign policy priorities, relations with Russia and the Kosovo issue, as Serbia's new political leadership faces growing expectations to clarify its position on the country's European future.

The exclusive interview on Europe Today, Euronews' morning show, came on the day of the EU-Western Balkans summit, which Serbia's speaker of the Parliament and acting president, Aleksandar Čupić, was expected to attend but ultimately could not, informing the European Commission of his absence.

Asked why Brussels should believe that Serbia's new political leadership is serious about European integration if it could not be represented at such an important gathering, el Sarag said that the country's parliamentary proceedings had to take priority.

"Because today we have to finish a constitutive session and that is our priority right now. And I hope it will finish today and the call for him is going to repeat again. It's nothing personal. We have to do this kind of thing first," she explained, adding that she was sorry about the absence.

The reason for this refusal is technical in nature. Aleksandar Čupić is currently the only official from the new administration to have been elected to his position as Speaker of Parliament and to be serving as Acting President of the Republic, given that Aleksandar Vučić submitted his resignation in September. Simply, there is no one who can come.

Asked whether the European Union was genuinely committed to admitting new members or whether enlargement was increasingly becoming a political slogan, el Sarag argued that political changes were already taking place in Serbia, although more time would be needed to demonstrate the direction of the new leadership.

"I think that we changed something, we changed the mind in the people's head in Serbia, which is something new in the political scene. And I think we need a little time to prove where we are going," she said.

However, questions about Serbia's future foreign policy alignment with the EU revealed some of the uncertainties surrounding the Students' List's position. Asked whether Serbia would align its foreign policy with Brussels, including imposing sanctions on Russia, or continue balancing its relations between Brussels and Moscow, el Sarag rejected the premise of the question.

"I think that question is not correct, because we don't want to make enemies. We want to be friends with all countries, if it's possible, of course," she said.

When pressed on how Serbia could become an EU member while maintaining relations with Russia, whose president, Vladimir Putin, is regarded by the EU as a major threat to European security, el Sarag questioned why European integration should require Serbia to make enemies.

"I'm a lawyer, you know, and that kind of question, I don't know why we must be enemies with somebody if we are including in European Union. Why we must take the side," she responded.

After the interviewer pointed to Russia's actions against European countries, including alleged violations of airspace and hybrid attacks, and asked whether Serbia intended to join the EU while maintaining close ties with Putin, el Sarag clarified that she had not advocated such a position.

"No, I didn't say that. I think that we are going to make some kind of solution in the future in that question," she said, without specifying what such a solution might entail.

The Kosovo issue also exposed the lack of a clearly articulated position. Asked whether Serbia would be prepared to fundamentally change its stance on Kosovo as part of the process of normalizing relations, a key element of its EU accession path, el Sarag said that the decision should come from the citizens rather than the Students' List.

"I think that people from Serbia are going to give that kind of answer, not me or nobody from the Student's list," she said.

When asked what she believed that answer would be, she added: "I don't know, we are in the parliament for five days, but I think Kosovo is Serbia."

Confronted with the observation that people in Kosovo and EU institutions hold a different position, el Sarag maintained that there was no need to rush the discussion.

"We will see, don't hurry, we are not in hurry now," she concluded.

The interview highlighted the challenges facing Serbia's new political representatives as they seek to establish their position on European integration. While el Sarag expressed confidence that political attitudes in Serbia were changing and stressed the importance of maintaining friendly relations with all countries, her answers left several key questions unresolved, particularly regarding alignment with EU foreign policy, relations with Russia and the future of dialogue with Kosovo.

The road ahead for relations between Serbia and the European Union is likely to be a particularly bumpy one, regardless of the political changes currently taking place in Belgrade. Two major issues will continue to dominate the relationship and remain the proverbial elephants in the room: Kosovo and Serbia's refusal to impose sanctions on Russia. On Kosovo, there is no indication that Serbia is prepared to recognize its independence, while Brussels continues to insist on substantial progress towards the normalization of relations.

On Russia, Serbia's unwillingness to align with EU sanctions following the invasion of Ukraine represents an equally serious obstacle, particularly as Brussels increasingly expects candidate countries to demonstrate a clear geopolitical commitment to the Union.

However, the difficulties will not be limited to foreign policy. The student movement, which has emerged as a significant political force in Serbia, is itself deeply suspicious of the European Union and, in particular, of Brussels' previous relationship with Aleksandar Vučić and his government. There is a widespread perception among the movement's supporters that EU institutions, and particularly the European Commission, were willing to turn a blind eye to the nature of Vučić's rule in the interest of maintaining political stability and preserving their relationship with Belgrade. For approximately 14 years, Brussels maintained close political relations with Vučić, despite mounting concerns about the state of democracy, media freedom, electoral conditions, institutional independence and the concentration of power in Serbia.

In this respect, it is important to distinguish between the positions of the different EU institutions. The European Parliament was consistently much more critical of the Serbian authorities, raising concerns about democratic backsliding and electoral irregularities and repeatedly calling for greater accountability. The European Commission, by contrast, generally adopted a considerably more accommodating approach, maintaining political engagement with Vučić's government and repeatedly assessing that Serbia had met the technical conditions for opening the next negotiating clusters.

Indeed, the Commission maintained for several consecutive years that Cluster 3, covering competitiveness and inclusive growth, was technically ready to be opened. Yet the European Council, where the member states ultimately make the political decisions on enlargement, never gave the green light to its opening. This created a rather contradictory situation in which the Commission continued to signal that progress was technically possible, while the member states were unwilling to translate that assessment into a political decision.

Consequently, the student movement inherits a complicated relationship with Brussels: it needs the EU politically, economically and institutionally, but it also has reasons to question the credibility and consistency of the Union's previous engagement with Serbia. The EU, for its part, will also have to accept that a new political generation in Serbia may be considerably less willing to accommodate Brussels' expectations without questioning the Union's own record and political choices.

Last year’s global health cuts are reversing the world's progress on HIV, UNAIDS said in a new report.

Hundreds of thousands of people lost access to HIV prevention drugs after wealthy countries cut foreign aid last year, according to the UN agency dedicated to HIV/AIDS.

The United States, United Kingdom, France and other major donors all slashed funding for global health programmes in 2025, which decimated HIV treatment and prevention in lower-income countries. About 41 million people globally had HIV in 2025, with 1.2 million new infections.

Overall, foreign aid to fight HIV fell by 18% in 2025 — the largest decline in almost two decades — while domestic funding increased by 4%, according to the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS (UNAIDS).

Countries in Western and Central Africa rely on foreign funding for about 90% of their HIV treatment services. But even countries with bigger domestic budgets still depend on donors to fund HIV prevention programmes.

Since the 2025 cuts, the number of people with access to pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) — an HIV prevention drug that protects people from infection if they are exposed to the virus — has fallen sharply, the UNAIDS report found. About 446,000 fewer people were on PrEP in 2025 than in 2024, though uptake increased in a few countries, including Brazil, Uganda and Tanzania.

UNAIDS estimates that only 2.6 million people worldwide had access to PrEP last year, while more than 20 million could benefit.

PrEP use plummeted among groups at higher risk of HIV infection: it fell by 59% among sex workers, 58% among people who inject drugs, 23% among transgender people and 17% among gay men and other men who have sex with men, the report found.

“We know what happens when HIV prevention collapses. People become infected, treatment needs rise, costs soar and lives are lost,” UNAIDS Executive Director Winnie Byanyima said.

“Every clinic that closes, every outreach worker who loses their job and every young woman turned away from prevention services today risks becoming a new HIV infection tomorrow,” she added.

PrEP is typically taken as a daily pill, which can make it difficult to access or stay on. Over the past year, countries have begun rolling out lenacapavir, an injectable form of PrEP that only has to be taken twice per year. By October, 175,000 people in nine sub-Saharan African countries had started on lenacapavir, UNAIDS said, and cheaper, generic versions are expected to become available next year.

Researchers are also developing other long-acting forms of PrEP, such as a once-monthly pill. But HIV experts have warned that global aid cuts will limit who can actually access these new medicines.

“It is unconscionable that just as the world has breakthrough prevention technologies capable of dramatically reducing new infections, funding cuts are putting those tools out of reach for the people who need them most,” Byanyima said.

Global health cuts are having an impact beyond HIV prevention, UNAIDS data shows. Fewer HIV tests are being done, making it harder to detect infections quickly and funnel people into treatment. Fewer HIV patients are starting antiretroviral therapy (ART), which suppresses their viral loads. And HIV surveillance has also taken a hit.

As a result, the ripple effects of last year's funding cuts will be felt for years to come, UNAIDS said

"The world is sleepwalking into a preventable crisis," Byanyima said.

Serbia's new Student List leadership will skip Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels and is not expected to sign its declaration, delaying clarity on whether Belgrade will align with EU foreign policy. Russia sanctions and Kosovo are the main sticking points.

Serbia's new political leadership will be conspicuously absent from Wednesday's summit between Western Balkan leaders and the EU institutions, leaving open whether the incoming government in Belgrade will align more closely with the bloc's foreign policy.

Importantly, given its absence, Brussels also does not expect Serbia to subscribe to the summit's declaration, which reiterates commitments to EU values and rejects historical revisionism and the glorification of war crimes.

In September, the mass funeral attended by senior Serbian government officials for convicted war criminal Ratko Mladić, known as the Butcher of Bosnia, attracted strong criticism from the EU and several member states.

The non-appearance of the region's largest and most influential country casts a shadow on the Brussels summit, as the EU seeks to capitalise on renewed enlargement momentum and deepen its ties with the Western Balkans.

Aleksandar Čupić, Serbia's newly elected parliamentary speaker and acting president, was invited but was unavailable due to parliamentary business, including setting up committees and preparing to call presidential elections.

"Today we have to finish a constitutive session, and that is our priority right now," Sarah El Sarag, a Student List MP, told Euronews. "It's nothing personal. We have to do this kind of thing first."

The absence is all the more significant because Serbia is in political transition after Aleksandar Vučić's ruling party lost power after 14 years.

The Student List, the protest movement's electoral vehicle, now holds a parliamentary majority and is expected to form the next government.

But skipping the summit means Brussels must wait longer to learn how the new leadership intends to position Serbia on the bloc's most sensitive foreign-policy issues, above all Russia.

Serbia's absence has also become somewhat of a common feature at these summits. In December 2025, Vučić announced that neither he nor any other Serbian official would attend the EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels, protesting EU member states' failure to agree to open Cluster 3 of Serbia's accession talks.

"The alignment with the EU's common foreign and security policy really remains a number one pressing issue. In the current geopolitical context, our member states expect a clear strategic orientation from partners who aspire to join the European Union, both in words and in deeds," an EU official told reporters ahead of Wednesday's summit.

In other words, Brussels has been tightening the screws on how far candidate countries must align with the bloc's foreign policy, as Euronews has previously reported.

The European External Action Service, the EU's diplomatic arm, has instructed EU delegations to closely monitor the implementation of sanctions against Russia and possible circumvention in candidate countries.

Joining the EU's sanctions regime against Moscow would be a particularly difficult decision for Serbia. Student List representatives have voiced support for speeding up accession, notably through reforms of the rule of law, judicial independence and media freedom, but have so far avoided committing to any shift in foreign policy.

At a meeting with senior EU officials in Brussels, representatives of the new parliamentary majority said their commitment to internal reforms was driven primarily by the interests of Serbian citizens rather than by the goal of European integration, as the movement campaigned on an anti-corruption platform.

Sanctions on Russia are likely to become a major source of friction between the future government and Brussels. A Eurobarometer survey published in May found that 67% of Serbian respondents opposed sanctions against the Russian government, individuals and companies.

Opposition has deep historical roots. UN sanctions on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, during the wars in the former Yugoslavia, contributed to economic hardship, hyperinflation and international isolation.

NATO's 1999 bombing campaign and Russia's later diplomatic backing for Belgrade, particularly over Kosovo, further shaped public attitudes towards Western foreign policy.

In an interview with Radio Free Europe last month, Ilija Srdanović, who has emerged as the Student List's main international interlocutor, said Serbian citizens should ultimately decide the country's position on sanctions against Russia through an open public debate.

Another potential source of friction is the widespread perception within the protest movement that EU institutions and several European leaders accommodated Vučić despite the repression of demonstrations, corruption and curbs on media freedom.

As recently as July 2026, the Commission renewed its push to open Cluster 3 for EU accession, but eight member states blocked it, largely over Belgrade's ambiguous position on Russia and its domestic reform record.

Kosovo could further complicate relations with the new leadership. Serbia's refusal to recognise its independence, and its reliance on Russian diplomatic support to keep Kosovo from wider international recognition, remain significant obstacles to normalisation.

Here, too, Srdanović has sought a balance. He has said the Student List is committed to continuing the EU-facilitated dialogue between Belgrade and Pristina, while arguing that agreements reached by previous Serbian governments should be reviewed for compliance with the constitution.

That raises questions about the movement's willingness to implement the 2023 Ohrid Agreement, under which Serbia committed not to oppose Kosovo's membership of international organisations.

"Our expectation remains that Serbia, like all the other partners in the region, aligns with the EU common foreign and security policy," a second EU official said.

For Brussels, the challenge is to establish whether the new leadership's commitment to democratic reform can translate into a broader strategic reorientation, or whether Serbia's foreign policy will stay largely unchanged despite the upheaval in Belgrade.

It's been a great year for cinema when it comes to numbers, with Summer 2026 officially delivering the biggest box office since COVID thanks to The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day, as well as breakout hits like Obsession and Backrooms. And the year isn't over yet...

In little over three weeks' time, two of the year's biggest blockbusters drop on the same day: Dune: Part 3 and Avengers: Doomsday. When it comes to the latter, it looks like Hollywood's bean counters will be rubbing their hands once more...

The final Doomsday trailer dropped yesterday, and it racked up 563 million views in its first 24 hours – making it the most viewed Disney trailer of all time, beating the Avengers: Doomsday teaser (503 million in 24 hours). 

According to data from WaveMetrix (via Deadline), the final Doomsday promo was the second-most-viewed movie trailer of all time behind Sony/Marvel Studio’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day, which was watched by 718.6m in its first 24-hours, and wound up becoming 2026's biggest film. 

Considering final trailers usually get fewer views compared to first trailers, it seems like Doomsday is bound to set a box office opening record. Not long to find out now...

Meanwhile, Doomsday director Anthony Russo has spoken out on Patrick Stewart's last day on set. 

Doomsday will be Patrick Stewart's final on screen role, having died aged 86 on 28 October. Stewart had been "struggling with his health", Russo revealed to Entertainment Weekly.

“He worked so hard to deliver a performance and a presence - for us as directors, for his other actors, for the crew," said Russo. “You could see it wasn’t just the effort of a regular actor showing up and delivering that kind of presence and performance and experience for others, collaboration.”

Russo continued: “It was someone who was really being challenged in a very deep way on a health level, showing up and doing that. For him to have muscled through and delivered the performance that he did in that movie, and the experience that he delivered for all of us as collaborators, it made it intensely emotional.”

Marvel Studio president Kevin Feige also remembered Stewart’s last day on set, sharing that the actor “stood up and he gave a speech to the crew”.

“We didn’t know necessarily it would be his last day on a set, but he was sort of indicating to us that he thought it was,” he said.

Feige said Marvel was now considering how best to honour Stewart in the finished film, saying: “We’re long done filming that movie, and he did an amazing job for us. We’re looking now at how we can put something together that honors and respects our friend.”

Avengers: Doomsday will be Stewart's ninth and final appearance as Professor X.

The beloved actor first played Charles Xavier in the 2000 film X-Men. He went on to play the character in several instalments of the franchise, including X2 (2003), X-Men: The Last Stand (2006), X-Men: Days of Future Past (2014), and Logan (2017), before making a brief return in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness (2022).

Avengers: Doomsday hits theatres on 18 December.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar agreed that a new chapter had begun in relations between their two countries after years of hostility, as they met under maximum security on Tuesday in Ukraine's Transcarpathia region.

Both leaders said good-neighbourly relations were being restored.

The two men began by laying wreaths at the graves of fallen soldiers in a cemetery in Uzhhorod, western Ukraine. Zelenskyy said 316 soldiers had been buried there since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

After the ceremony, Magyar said the Hungarian government delegation had not come empty-handed. It brought patient-monitoring equipment, medicines and energy equipment such as generators, worth 1 billion forints, which may be needed during the cold winter months. Magyar stressed that Hungary has not supplied weapons to Ukraine.

Zelenskyy thanked the delegation for the aid. The two sides then moved on to the Old Continent hotel in Uzhhorod, where officials including Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán discussed further support for Ukraine and its possible European integration.

The two leaders had already met in person at EU and NATO gatherings, but Hungary had made an intergovernmental meeting conditional on its demands being met.

Magyar signalled that the meeting was imminent in a speech to the Hungarian parliament on Monday. In it, he recalled the hate-mongering election campaign that the government of his predecessor, Viktor Orbán, had run against Ukraine and Zelenskyy.

By contrast, Magyar told lawmakers, his new government stands by the Hungarians of Transcarpathia and the Ukrainian people under attack, even if Moscow objects.

The Hungarian government is no longer blocking Ukraine's EU accession

According to media reports, Hungary's government withdrew its objections to the last two groups of negotiating chapters, known as clusters, in Ukraine's EU accession process at last week's meeting of EU ambassadors. This means Ukraine and Moldova can now begin talks on every area of EU membership, including particularly sensitive ones such as the environment and agriculture.

Agriculture is a especially delicate issue for Kyiv. The European Commission, under pressure from Poland and France among others, has proposed limiting the access of certain Ukrainian farm products to EU funds and the European market.

Speaking to Euronews, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said Kyiv cannot accept its farmers being permanently shut out of the European market, and that any measures introduced must be temporary and proportionate.

Opening the negotiating clusters is only the beginning. Candidate countries must then bring their laws and practices into line with EU rules, and during that process member states can use their veto more than 100 times, halting progress.

Budapest held up Ukraine's accession process for a long time by blocking the opening of the negotiating clusters. Its veto also stalled Moldova's membership bid, which remains tied to Kyiv's.

Hungary's position began to change after Magyar replaced Viktor Orbán, who had been in power for 16 years. The first negotiating cluster was opened in June, the second in July and two more in October.

Last month, Kyiv and Budapest reached an agreement on the rights of the ethnic Hungarian minority in western Ukraine, which the Ukrainian parliament then adopted.

Although the Hungarian government was ready to move forward, it still waited a few weeks before agreeing to open the last two clusters. Years of anti-Ukrainian rhetoric from the Orbán government had made the step politically difficult at home.

On 16 October, on the sidelines of the European Council summit in Brussels, Belgium, the Hungarian side and Zelenskyy held their first bilateral meeting, another step towards better relations between the two neighbours.

Dacă ai posibilitatea de a alege între un acumulator de 7, 14 sau 21 kWh, varianta de 21 kWh poate părea cea mai bună la prima vedere. Ai mai multă energie disponibilă, deci de ce ai alege o capacitate mai mică?

În realitate, lucrurile stau altfel. Capacitatea potrivită pentru un sistem fotovoltaic depinde de cât produce acesta, cât consumă locuința și, mai ales, în ce momente ale zilei apar producția și consumul.

Ce înseamnă 7, 14 și 21 kWh în cazul Huawei LUNA?

Configurațiile bateriilor fotovoltaice Huawei LUNA sunt bazate pe modulul LUNA2000-7-E1, care oferă 6,9 kWh de energie utilizabilă.

Un singur modul formează configurația LUNA2000-7-S1. Două module oferă 13,8 kWh, iar trei ajung la 20,7 kWh. Această construcție modulară are o consecință importantă: nu trebuie neapărat să pornești direct cu cea mai mare configurație.

Dar de unde știi ce capacitate îți trebuie?

Verifică mai întâi surplusul de energie

Să presupunem că panourile produc într-o zi 20 kWh, iar locuința consumă direct 14 kWh în intervalul respectiv. Surplusul disponibil pentru stocare este de aproximativ 6 kWh.

Într-un asemenea scenariu simplificat, instalarea unei baterii mult mai mari doar pentru că aceasta oferă o capacitate superioară nu înseamnă automat că vei utiliza acea capacitate.

Pe de altă parte, o locuință cu producție fotovoltaică mai mare, consum redus în timpul zilei și consum ridicat seara poate avea un surplus suficient pentru o configurație de stocare mai mare.

Prin urmare, trebuie urmărite cel puțin două curbe: producția sistemului și consumul locuinței.

Specialiștii din echipa Genway insistă tocmai asupra acestui principiu și recomandă prosumatorilor analiza datelor reale din FusionSolar pentru identificarea consumului de bază, a vârfurilor de consum, a surplusului disponibil și a necesarului energetic din timpul nopții – desigur, înainte de a alege un acumulator fotovoltaic.

Mai există un aspect care poate fi ușor trecut cu vederea!

Capacitatea exprimată în kWh arată câtă energie poate stoca bateria. Puterea exprimată în kW arată, simplificat, cât de repede poate aceasta să primească sau să furnizeze energie.

În cazul configurațiilor LUNA2000 de 7, 14 și 21 kWh, puterea maximă de încărcare și descărcare crește odată cu numărul modulelor: aproximativ 3,5 kW pentru un modul, 7 kW pentru două și 10,5 kW pentru trei.

Prin urmare, două locuințe cu același consum zilnic pot avea nevoi diferite dacă una dintre ele are vârfuri de consum mult mai mari.

Cum ajungi la configurația potrivită?

Nu există o regulă universală de tipul „un sistem fotovoltaic de X kWp necesită automat o baterie de Y kWh”.

Trebuie analizate producția existentă, energia consumată direct, surplusul injectat în rețea, consumul după apus și eventualele schimbări viitoare – de exemplu, instalarea unui nou electrocasnic sau încărcarea unei mașini electrice.

În acest context, este utilă modularitatea Huawei LUNA. Sistemul poate începe cu un modul și poate fi extins prin adăugarea altor module compatibile, Huawei folosind optimizarea individuală la nivelul acestora.

Genway include în oferta de stocare analiza necesară și instalarea sistemului, iar specialiștii recomandă alegerea acumulatorului după curba reală de producție și consum. Colaborarea cu Genway îți pune la dispoziție experiența a peste 13.800 de proiecte fotovoltaice gestionate în totalitate – de la proiectare până la racordare!

Prin urmare, întrebarea potrivită nu este neapărat „cât de mare poate fi bateria?”, ci „câtă energie este disponibilă pentru stocare și cât consum atunci când panourile nu mai produc?”.

Răspunsul la aceste două întrebări te poate ajuta să înțelegi dacă ai nevoie de 7, 14 sau 21 kWh pentru locuința ta.

Talks to give Britain access to the EU's electricity market are under way, but Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands are among those insisting London pays in first.

Millions of British households will pay around £443 (€527) more a year for energy from January, after UK regulator Ofgem raised its price cap by 26%, blaming the war in the Middle East.

The typical annual bill will rise to about £2,166 (€2,578) under the new cap. Ofgem sets the cap every quarter, and it limits what suppliers can charge for gas and electricity.

About 20 million households on standard variable tariffs will feel the rise. Another 10 million on fixed-rate deals won't be affected until their contracts end.

"Conflict in the Middle East continues to drive energy costs higher, and we know this price increase will be a worry for many households as winter approaches," said Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets.

The US-Iran war broke out on 28 February and has sharply reduced tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, pushing up oil and gas prices. European natural gas, measured by the Dutch TTF futures contract, has climbed by around 190% since then, from about €32 to €92 per megawatt-hour.

How UK bills compare with Europe

From January, British households will pay around 70% more for electricity than the average household in the EU.

Once standing charges are included, a typical British household will pay about €48.40 per 100 kWh, based on XE's exchange rate of £1 = €1.19. The EU average was €28.30 in the first half of 2026, according to Eurostat, and the most expensive country in the bloc, Ireland, charged €38.70.

The gap is narrower for gas. British households will pay about €14.40 per 100 kWh, against an EU average of €11.00.

The UK is already in talks with Brussels to join the EU's internal electricity market, a move supporters say would boost energy security and make electricity trading easier. But five EU countries, including Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands, have demanded that Britain contribute financially to cohesion funds, which aim to narrow gaps between EU regions, in return, Euronews reported earlier this month.

Martin McCluskey, the UK's energy minister, said the UK is still working to understand the EU's proposal and that no amount has been agreed. McCluskey added that any payment must deliver "value for money."

The price rise comes despite support measures announced in October in Prime Minister Andy Burnham's annual budget. These included a one-off £100 payment (€119) towards energy bills for 20 million households and the removal of fixed fees on gas bills. Burnham's government has also extended a temporary tax cut on household electricity prices.

Many households will still end up paying more even after the subsidy.

The increase is also likely to push inflation higher next year. The UK's annual inflation rate hit a 12-month high of 3.6% in October, driven by higher motor fuel costs linked to the conflict.

Gas prices are still well below their peak during the 2022 energy crisis, which followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The biggest increase to the price cap came in October 2022, when it went up by 80%.

What if you could step back into your childhood and see the world exactly as you did then? In Marrakech, one French artist is doing just that by presenting upside-down houses, giant furniture and surreal, wildly imaginative sculptures.

At Ramakech, an outdoor sculpture park located on the outskirts of the Moroccan city, visitors can immerse themselves in the work of Jean-François Fourtou, whose sculptures draw heavily on memories of childhood, family and the way we experience the world as children.

Perhaps the star attraction of the 11-hectare park is 'The house that fell from the sky'. Created in 2010, the house is completely inverted, with furniture, windows and bathroom fixtures turned upside down, giving the impression that, as the title suggests, it's come and crash landed onto its roof.

"'The house that fell from the sky' is the house where my grandfather died more than 30 years ago. He was a very important figure throughout my childhood, inspiring me and shaping the way I express myself artistically, including the way I do today. So, I wanted to pay tribute to him," says Fourtou.

He adds: "To me, it is as if he had sent this house back to me from the sky. It was a small rented house in Charente-Maritime, where he used to spend his summers."

Childhood is a theme that runs throughout the park, with many of Fourtou's installations drawing on the strange, exaggerated way the world can feel when you're a child.

His 'Giant House' is one of the first installations he created for the site, featuring oversized furniture and everyday objects, from chairs and tables to notebooks, pens and clothing. Visitors are encouraged to release their inner child and climb, sit and interact with the objects.

"I wanted to recapture the feelings I had when I was four years old, staying at my great-grandmother’s house in a village in the south of France. There was barely any running water, no bathroom, and everything was very rustic. I have wonderful memories of that place, and I wanted to rediscover those childhood sensations," explains Fourtou.

Elsewhere, there's also a wonderfully whimsical take on the natural world, with sculptures of farmers and gardeners with enormous heads inspired by vegetables and plants. They can be found scattered throughout the park, tending the land, climbing trees and resting in the shade. There are also a few oversized ants to be found crawling around the landscape.

As Fourtou puts it: "Art is something deeply emotional, and that is what I seek to convey through my work. For me, it is certainly a form of therapy, not a nostalgia for childhood, but rather a way of understanding, expressing and reconnecting with important fundamental values."

He began transforming the site into a space for his artwork in 1999, with the park opening to the public in 2024. It now attracts around 5,000 visitors every year.

Almost one in three Europeans say they cannot afford the upfront cost of installing a heat pump.

For Europeans worried about how much it will cost to heat their homes this winter, switching to a heat pump is an attractive prospect.

That is, if they can get past the cost of installing one.

Interest in heat pumps is growing across Europe – especially in households struggling to pay their energy bills - according to a survey of 6,000 people in France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Poland and the UK.

But almost one in three said they can’t afford the upfront installation costs, making it the most cited obstacle to making the switch.

How much can heat pumps save on energy bills?

Heat pumps, which work by capturing energy from air, water or the ground and turning it into heat or cold air, typically deliver three to four kWh of heat for every one kilowatt-hour (kWh) of electricity they consume. Once they are installed, they can have a big impact on your bottom line.

According to the IEA, heat pumps are cheaper to run than gas boilers in almost every EU country, offering annual energy savings of up to €800.

When used effectively, air-source heat pumps could heat homes for as little as €2.20 on a typical winter day, according to British property developer Barratt Redrow.

Jean-Paul Harreman, director at market intelligence provider Montel, says that, even in very cold weather, “the efficiency is better from a heat pump than from a gas boiler.”

How much does it cost to install a heat pump?

Making the switch still requires investment. Installing a heat pump can cost several thousands euros more than a gas boiler. Often, the installation costs as much as the equipment itself, if not more.

In the UK, the average cost of installing an air-source heat pump was about €15,000 in 2025 – five times the cost of installing a new gas boiler.

And the prices are not uniform across the continent, either. In Germany, it can cost up to €40,000. Much of that difference boils down to the equipment, Jan Rosenow, a professor of energy and climate policy at the University of Oxford, explained in a recent analysis.

Germany’s heat pump market is dominated by more expensive European manufacturers, while cheaper brands – including some sourced from Asia – are more widely available in the UK, France and the Netherlands.

Stricter installation requirements and taxation are also factors. For example, Germany charges 19 per cent VAT on heat pump installations, while the UK scrapped VAT on them in 2022. Some homes may also need to have their radiators replaced or their electrical systems upgraded, which adds to the bill.

But labour, Rosenow added, is not a major factor in prices. “We expected labour costs to make a big difference but were surprised to find that they didn’t.”

That leaves room for installation prices to come down as equipment becomes cheaper.

How to lower heat pump prices

There are many ways to mitigate the costs, however.

Across Europe, governments are offering grants, tax breaks and low-interest loans to encourage homeowners to switch to greener heating.

In England and Wales, eligible homeowners can receive a grant of around €8,500 towards installation. France, Germany and Italy also offer financial assistance to make the switch.

But for people already struggling to pay their bills, even reduced prices may be unaffordable.

Three-quarters of respondents in the poll, commissioned by the European Climate Foundation, said rising living and energy costs have affected their budgets, and two-thirds expect to heat some rooms less this winter. Yet fewer than half say they are likely to invest in home improvements or energy-saving equipment.

Paying subsidies in advance rather than reimbursing after heat pumps are installed is one possible solution. Nearly six in 10 respondents in Verian’s survey say they would back such a measure. In fact, the idea received majority support in all six countries.

Homeowners can also save money by shopping around. The UK’s Energy Saving Trust recommends getting quotes from at least three qualified installers, as well as having your home assessed to ensure you are not paying for a more powerful heat pump than you need.

Choosing a speciality electricity tariff or installing solar panels to generate some of the electricity needed to run your heat pump can also offset costs and lower bills.

Even if Europeans are warming up to heat pumps, the need to “[make] the financial benefits clearer and more immediate for households”, as the Verian study revealed, might be growing just as quickly.

Spain's economy is forecast to grow more than twice as fast as the eurozone's this year, but average pay still buys less than it did in 2009. Rising housing and food costs are putting household budgets under pressure ahead of Sunday's election.

Average wages in Spain were still below their 2009 peak last year after being adjusted for inflation, even as the economy continued to outgrow most of its European peers.

Spain's economy is forecast to grow by 2.6% this year, more than twice the eurozone's projected 1.2%, according to the European Commission. But that growth has brought only modest gains in average real pay since Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez took office in 2018.

The gap between a fast-growing economy and what households can afford has become a campaign issue ahead of Sunday's snap election. Sánchez has pointed to Spain's strong growth while acknowledging voters' concerns about the cost of living. His main rival, conservative Popular Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, has accused the government of doing too little and pledged to cut personal income tax in his first year in office.

Five figures show how wages, food prices and housing costs have shaped what Spaniards can afford.

2009

That was the peak for Spain's inflation-adjusted average annual wage in the OECD series. In 2025, the average was €35,121, about 1% below the 2009 peak of €35,533 and about 5% above its 2018 level.

Economists say much of Spain's growth in recent years has been driven by immigration, with new arrivals expanding the labour force. Sánchez has defended his immigration-friendly policies as a way to maintain Spain's large social welfare system. Many immigrants fill critical jobs in agriculture, tourism and other industries, but often in low-paying positions.

“What’s happening is that we have more people working,” said Pedro Aznar, an economist at the Barcelona-based Esade Business School. "We have a larger working population contributing to GDP, but our growth is driven more by volume rather than by generating more output per worker.”

Minimum-wage earners are an exception. Their wages have grown 66% since Sánchez took office in 2018, leaving them better off even after inflation.

45%

While housing has become the focus of public discontent in Spain, food prices also rose substantially, by 45% between 2015 and 2025, according to AP. The government has at various points cut VAT on food, subsidised energy and provided financial support to households.

Analysts say cost increases around food and energy were driven partly by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.

“Since the war in Ukraine began, we have experienced significant spikes in inflation, and at many points, the rate of inflation has outpaced wage growth,” Aznar said. “Consequently, even if wages rise, if inflation increases by a greater margin, the worker loses purchasing power.”

Conservative opposition leader Feijóo has made the rising cost of living a key campaign issue, promising to lower personal income tax within his first year in office, and criticising Sánchez for often highlighting Spain's GDP growth.

Talavera said rising costs have left many Spaniards who were employed in 2018 feeling poorer now because their money simply doesn't go as far.

“In economic terms, that is the main story.”

43%

House prices in Spain rose 43% between 2015 and 2025 when adjusted for inflation, according to Eurostat’s house price index. Across the European Union, prices rose an average of 25% during the same period.

Market pressures and insufficient construction have driven prices even higher in Spain's largest cities and popular tourist destinations, putting homeownership beyond the reach of many young Spaniards.

Spain has a strong tradition of homeownership, but the Bank of Spain estimates the country of 50 million people has a shortage of 750,000 houses based on demand and the pace of new construction.

Homebuilding fell sharply after the 2008 financial crisis ended a construction boom. Large investors bought property in the aftermath, contributing to speculation in later years. Sánchez and Feijóo have both promised financial help for first-time buyers if elected.

Two-thirds

About two-thirds of people aged 18 to 34 in Spain were still living with their parents in 2025, according to figures from Spain's National Statistics Institute. Among 26- to 34-year-olds who lived with their parents, 47.3% said the main reason was that they could not afford to rent or buy a home.

Rents across Spain have also risen by 43% over the past decade, with the largest increases in cities and coastal areas. Population growth has increased demand, while the spread of short-term tourist lets on platforms such as Airbnb and Booking.com has reduced the supply of homes available to long-term renters in some areas.

1 in 4

That’s roughly the share of renters in Spain who spend more than 40% of their income on housing, excluding those who receive government-subsidised or free housing. Spain has a higher proportion of overburdened renters than other major European Union economies, including Germany, France, and Italy.

In cities like Madrid and Barcelona, many renters fork over an even larger share of their income every month.

“You have a big chunk of the population that essentially has seen their income in real terms go down because prices have gone up more than their wages," said Ángel Talavera, an economist who studies Europe at Oxford Economics. “Housing has gone, well, bananas.”

So, which countries had the highest and lowest average salaries? How do the rankings change when purchasing power is taken into account? And how do experts explain the differences?

Luxembourg pays the most

Across the 26 EU countries in Eurostat's ranking, average gross full-time adjusted salaries ranged from €16,201 in Bulgaria to €85,609 in Luxembourg, more than five times Bulgaria's figure.

Among the remaining countries, Denmark (€73,500), Ireland (€64,387), Belgium (€61,984) and Austria (€60,727) had the highest average salaries, rounding out the top five, all above €60,000.

Germany leads the 'Big Four'

Among the EU's 'Big Four' economies, Germany had the highest average salary at €56,360. France was just above the EU average at €44,734.

Gross full-time pay was much lower in the bloc's third- and fourth-largest economies, at €34,213 in Italy and €35,125 in Spain.

Other countries above the EU average included Finland (€50,960) and Sweden (€49,622).

At the bottom of the list, Bulgaria has the lowest average salary at €16,201. Greece (€18,772) and Hungary (€20,138) follow. Romania (€20,818), Slovakia (€21,661) and Latvia (€22,688) are also among the lowest.

These are gross salaries, and net earnings or incomes can vary because of differences in taxes and social contributions between countries.

The pay gap narrows once local prices are taken into account

The purchasing power standard (PPS) is a unit used to compare what money can buy across countries. It removes the effect of price differences across countries, so one PPS buys the same amount of goods and services everywhere.

The gap narrows when salaries are adjusted for differences in household prices, according to Euronews Business calculations using Eurostat data.

The highest average salary is about three times the lowest, compared with more than five times in euros.

Luxembourg still ranks first with 65,106 PPS. Bulgaria moves up two places to 24th, while Greece ranks last with 21,486 PPS.

The ranking also changes substantially. Slovenia moves above the EU average, while Sweden and the bloc's second-largest economy, France, fall below it.

Poland and Lithuania each rise three places. Austria moves from fifth to second place. Denmark falls from second to fourth, and Ireland from third to sixth.

Several Central and Eastern European countries move up in the PPS ranking. Romania climbs from 23rd to 18th place, the biggest rise at five places.

Estonia has the biggest drop, falling from 16th to 21st place.

Why do salaries differ so much?

According to experts, the main reasons are differences in economic development and productivity.

"By and large, of course, the main reason for the differences in wages across European countries is the different levels of economic development and productivity, and the output created by workers," Jaan Masso, associate professor in applied econometrics at the University of Tartu, told Euronews Business.

Štěpán Jurajda, professor at CERGE-EI in Prague, pointed to similar factors. "The main reasons for the large gaps in salaries across European countries include different endowments of physical and human capital (education) and different productivity (including institutions, effective regulation, R&D policies etc.)," he told Euronews Business.

Labour market rules also play a significant role. Masso said minimum wages and collective agreements affect how equal wages are. He noted that "typically wages are much more equal in the Scandinavian countries".

Why are prices higher in rich countries?

Jurajda explained that richer countries usually have higher prices. "A basic empirical fact is that as countries become richer, their price level rises," he said.

Masso gave an example from the services sector. In some services, productivity cannot rise much. "One still needs similar time to cut hair," he said. So in high-wage countries, higher labour costs lead to higher prices for services.

"Naturally, for people living in a particular country, the price-adjusted figure is more relevant," Masso added.

Jurajda urged caution when reading the rankings. "In general, small PPP-adjusted differences should not be interpreted as precise country rankings," he said.

Is the East-West gap closing?

Malte Lübker, a wage expert at the Institute of Economic and Social Research (WSI) at the Hans Böckler Foundation, said the gap has narrowed.

"In the past, employers in high-wage countries have often pointed at lower wages in Eastern Europe to call for domestic wage restraint. However, the gap has closed considerably over time," he told Euronews Business.

Lübker said that this also affects migration. "When you adjust for purchasing power, taking up a job in Germany is no longer such an attractive proposition for Polish workers," he said.

What do full-time salaries not show?

Adjusting salaries to full-time equivalents makes comparisons easier. But experts say it has limitations.

"Converting wage data into full-time equivalents is, of course, a useful statistical technique. However, we should not forget that full-time work might not be readily available," Lübker said.

"For others, primarily women, part-time employment is the only way to reconcile work and care responsibilities. This means that full-time wages are an imperfect proxy for living standards."

Masso noted that part-time work varies a lot across Europe. In many Eastern European countries, full-time work has been the norm, while in the Netherlands part-time work is very common.

Experts also point out that averages can hide large differences within a country. Masso said that in Luxembourg, "the high average might be affected by a smaller number of very highly paid jobs, e.g., in the financial sector".

A Swedish research team set out to identify who could benefit most from taking vitamin D supplements.

Low vitamin D in the summertime may be a bigger red flag for your health than in the winter months, a new study has found.

Vitamin D helps the body regulate calcium and phosphate in the body, keeping our bones, teeth and muscles healthy. Most of it comes from sunlight, while people can also get some vitamin D from foods such as oily fish, eggs and some mushrooms. Millions of Europeans also take vitamin D supplements, though randomised trials have largely failed to show that routine supplementation improves health or boosts longevity.

Researchers from Uppsala University in Sweden wondered if seasonal swings in vitamin D levels might help explain why. In Europe and much of the Northern Hemisphere, people build up stores of vitamin D in their fat during the sunny summer months, and they may draw on those reserves as their vitamin D levels naturally fall in the darker winter months.

“We need to better understand who truly needs vitamin D supplementation,” the researchers wrote.

To find out, the researchers analysed vitamin D levels in the blood of more than 12,000 older people in Sweden. They split participants into groups based on whether their blood was drawn in summer, from July to September, or in winter, from January to March.

People with low vitamin D levels in summer were more likely to fracture a bone or die over the next 11 years, on average, than those with high summer levels. Meanwhile, people who had low vitamin D levels in the winter months were not at increased risk of bone fracture or death, according to the study, which was published in the journal PLOS Medicine.

People were considered to have low vitamin D if their blood concentration was below 40 nanomoles per litre (nmo/L) and high levels if it was above 80 nmol/L.

The findings suggest summer could be the best time to test vitamin D levels. That could help doctors identify people who are chronically low and could benefit the most from supplements, the researchers said.

“We should think carefully about when we measure vitamin D,” the researchers wrote. “Winter measurements are heavily influenced by seasonal variation, whereas low vitamin D levels during summer are more likely to reflect persistently low vitamin D status and a higher risk of adverse health outcomes.”

This was an observational study, meaning it cannot show whether low vitamin D levels cause bone fractures or early death. It was also conducted mainly in white Swedish people, so the results may not directly apply to other groups. Still, the findings held even after the researchers accounted for age, sex, body size and other factors.

The researchers said more randomised trials are needed to identify the potential health benefits of supplements, ideally focused on people with low vitamin D levels in the summer.
